## Proposition 5.18
**Statement:** If magnitudes be proportional separando, they will also be proportional componendo.

**Step 1.** Let the magnitudes be AB and CD, cut at E and F respectively, and let them be proportional separando. By D5.15 this means that, as AE (the excess of AB over EB) is to EB, so is CF (the excess of CD over FD) to FD. It is to be shown that they are also proportional componendo, that is, by D5.14, that as AB is to BE, so is CD to FD.

**Step 2.** Let G, H be any equimultiples whatever of AB, CD, each the m-th multiple, and let K, L be any equimultiples whatever of BE, FD, each the n-th multiple. By D5.5 it suffices to show that G exceeds, is equal to, or falls short of K according as H exceeds, is equal to, or falls short of L.

**Step 3.** Take P, Q, the m-th multiples of AE, EB, and R, S, the m-th multiples of CF, FD. Since P, Q are equimultiples of the parts AE, EB of the whole AB, their sum P + Q is the same multiple of AB (5.1); hence P + Q = G. Likewise R + S = H.

**Step 4.** Suppose first that n is not greater than m. If n = m, then K = Q and L = S. If n < m, then Q, the m-th multiple of EB, is the sum of the n-th multiple K of EB and the (m − n)-th multiple of EB (5.2), so that K is a part of Q and K < Q (CN5); likewise L < S. In either case K is not greater than Q and L is not greater than S. But Q is a part of G = P + Q, so Q < G (CN5); therefore K < G. Likewise S is a part of H = R + S, so S < H and therefore L < H. Thus G > K and H > L, and the two comparisons agree.

**Step 5.** Suppose next that n is greater than m. Let T, U be the (n − m)-th multiples of EB, FD. Then T + Q, the sum of the (n − m)-th and the m-th multiples of EB, is the n-th multiple of EB (5.2), so that K = T + Q; likewise L = U + S. Now P, R are equimultiples of AE, CF, and T, U are equimultiples of EB, FD; and since, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD, it follows by D5.5 that P exceeds, is equal to, or falls short of T according as R exceeds, is equal to, or falls short of U.

**Step 6.** If P = T, then R = U; adding Q to P and to T, and S to R and to U, we obtain P + Q = T + Q and R + S = U + S (CN2), that is, G = K and H = L. If P > T, then R > U; let P exceed T by X and R exceed U by Y, so that P = T + X and R = U + Y; then G = P + Q = (T + Q) + X = K + X and H = R + S = (U + S) + Y = L + Y, so K is a part of G and L a part of H, whence G > K and H > L (CN5). If P < T, then R < U; let T exceed P by X and U exceed R by Y; then K = T + Q = (P + Q) + X = G + X and L = U + S = (R + S) + Y = H + Y, whence G < K and H < L (CN5). Thus in every subcase G exceeds, is equal to, or falls short of K according as H exceeds, is equal to, or falls short of L.

**Step 7.** Therefore, G, H being any equimultiples whatever of AB, CD, and K, L any equimultiples whatever of BE, FD, the former equimultiples alike exceed, are alike equal to, or alike fall short of the latter equimultiples respectively taken in corresponding order. Hence, by D5.5, as AB is to BE, so is CD to FD; that is, by D5.14, the magnitudes are proportional componendo. Q.E.D.

**Remark on path.** The converse could also be approached by reductio through 5.17 (supposing that AB is to BE as CD is to some magnitude other than FD, separating, and deriving a contradiction), but that route presupposes the existence of a fourth proportional to three given magnitudes, which none of the available tools supplies. The proof above therefore proceeds directly from D5.5, mirroring the method used for 5.17.

**USED:** 5.1, 5.2, CN2, CN5, D5.14, D5.15, D5.5
**Human refs (from References field):** 5.11, 5.14, 5.17

heath_proof_text: Let AE, EB, CF, FD be magnitudes proportional separando, so that, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD; I say that they will also be proportional componendo, that is, as AB is to BE, so is CD to FD. For, if CD be not to DF as AB to BE, then, as AB is to BE, so will CD be either to some magnitude less than DF or to a greater. First, let it be in that ratio to a less magnitude DG. Then, since, as AB is to BE, so is CD to DG, they are magnitudes proportional componendo; so that they will also be proportional separando. [V. 17]  Therefore, as AE is to EB, so is CG to GD. But also, by hypothesis, as AE is to EB, so is CF to FD. Therefore also, as CG is to GD, so is CF to FD. [V. 11] But the first CG is greater than the third CF; therefore the second GD is also greater than the fourth FD. [V. 14]  But it is also less: which is impossible. Therefore, as AB is to BE, so is not CD to a less magnitude than FD. Similarly we can prove that neither is it in that ratio to a greater; it is therefore in that ratio to FD itself.
